newsitem.title: UK: Russia starts global blitz to woo investors.
newsitem.headline: Russia starts global blitz to woo investors.

text.p: Russia began a series of top level economic presentations around the world on Monday, with hopes of triggering a potential avalanche of demand for Russian assets.
Three teams of finance ministry and central bank officials will criss-cross the globe in what is thought to be the largest effort to woo investors of its kind.

"Turnout is expected to be huge, with hundreds of investors expected in London alone, because interest in Russia is so strong. All kinds of investors -- fixed-income and equity -- are very interested in hearing about Russia from senior officials," a banker familiar with the arrangements said.
"There will be questions about political and economic issues, other Russian debt instruments and all sorts of things."
Nearly two years after a Russian Eurobond was first mooted, investors will be able to ask officials, including Finance Minister Alexander Livshits, why they should invest in Russia.
With borrowers from Russia and other former Soviet republics queueing to raise funds, there is more at stake than whether the presentations lead to a successful bond issue for Russia alone.
"When Russia comes it will open a lot of doors," said a banker involved with another Russian borrower.
In line to launch bond issues are the cities of Moscow and St Petersburg, the republics of Kazakhstan and Ukraine, and Gazprom, the world's largest natural gas producer.

"Russia will be a benchmark for more than just other Russian borrowers," said a London Eurobond trader. "It sets a ceiling from a ratings point of view for former Soviet republics because many of the economies are closely tied to Russia."

On Monday officials and bankers from J.P. Morgan and SBC Warburg will meet investors in Tokyo and Luxembourg, hitting London on November 15 and ending the two-week promotional extravaganza in New York on November 20.
With President Boris Yeltsin itching to get back to work following his heart operation and months of inactivity, investors can at least be told the country has a leader.
"Yeltsin looking healthy on television gives some positive feeling to the presentations, but investment decisions do not hinge on his status alone," said a banker at a European bank.
More difficult questions include the status of International Monetary Fund (IMF) negotiations and the effect frozen MinFin bonds could have on Russia's credit ratings.
In October an IMF delegation left Moscow with no decision on whether to give Russia the latest tranche of a $10 billion loan.

The IMF was said to be worried about Russia's ability to repay other loans, although IMF Director General Michel Camdessus said on November 7 it was now working closely with the Russian government on solving the problem of tax collection.
"There is a question over the seizure of MinFin bonds. This is impacting people's perceptions here, and the situation has to be clarified," said a debt trader at a U.S. bank.
In October the Russian authorities said they had seized $74 million of dollar-denominated MinFin bonds this year, a further blow to the already illiquid sector.

This might encourage investors to buy an internationally listed, liquid Eurobond instead of investing in bonds like MinFins with custody in Russia, but might also raise worries about Russia's credit ratings, bankers said.
"If I were to buy a Russia Eurobond I would want to make sure they are not going to be in default on another bond," the U.S. bank's trader said.
Russia's long-term foreign currency debt was rated Ba2 by Moody's and BB-minus by Standard & Poor's, both below investment grade status but at the high end of market expectations.
Russia plans to launch the bond -- its first return to the international capital markets since the 1917 revolution -- by the end of November.
The deal is expected to be for up to $500 million with a five-year maturity. New issue traders said Russia hopes to pay no more than a 10 percent coupon for the funds.
